title: Hyperscaler integration risk and sales plays
content:
Purpose:
This note synthesizes technical integration risks customers encounter when choosing hyperscaler-managed endpoints (AWS/GCP/Azure) vs Redwood’s hosted/dedicated/private offering, and proposes concrete sales plays, objection handlers, and one-page battlecard language for field use. Focus is on platform/infra buyers (platform engineering, SRE, AI infra leads) evaluating long-term operational control, costs, and resilience trade offs.

Executive summary (elevator):
Hyperscaler endpoints look attractive for speed-to-prototype and single-pane console benefits, but buyers repeatedly run into persistence, latency tail risk, and operational lock-in that increase cost and complexity at scale. Redwood’s practical win is: same developer ergonomics + explicit operational controls (private plane, model version pinning, rollout semantics, and predictable reserved capacity) that reduce unknowns and migration costs for production applications.

Target personas and buying triggers:
- Platform engineering (primary) — cares about SLAs, observability, rate-limiting, network egress, and predictable unit economics.
- ML engineering (secondary) — cares about model fidelity, deterministic rollouts, eval regressions during model swaps.
- Security/compliance (influence) — needs KMS/HSM, VPC isolation, audit logs.
- Product managers (influence) — focused on latency SLOs, uptime, and cost-per-query.

Integration risk matrix (top-level):
- Data plane control: Hyperscalers: limited (black-boxed autoscaling, billing-linked throttles). Redwood: full options (hosted vs dedicated vs private VPC).
- Network and egress exposure: Hyperscalers: unpredictable egress costs & cross-region failover complexity. Redwood: placement choices + predictable reserved capacity to avoid surprise bills.
- Model lifecycle & rollouts: Hyperscalers: basic version pinning but limited rollout controls and canary tooling. Redwood: canary/A-B with automatic fallback and metric-driven rollback.
- Latency tail risk: Hyperscalers: noisy neighbor risk on shared endpoints, burst cold-starts. Redwood: dedicated pools, KV cache lifetime tuning, and routing by latency SLO.
- Compliance and data residency: Hyperscalers: region controls but often shared control plane. Redwood: private deployments and on-prem packages.

Typical pain patterns we’ve seen in the field (real examples to use in sales conversations):
- “Billing surprise” during marketing-driven spikes — sudden egress and per-request costs once product usage grows beyond PoC.
- “Model swap regression” that causes user-facing hallucinations because there was no staged rollout tied to evaluation sets.
- “Cross-region failover timeouts” on managed endpoints during cloud region maintenance windows.
- “SRE queues for vendor support” — long SLAs to change autoscaling or capacity reservations during an outage.

Competitor quick profiles (concise angles):
- AWS-managed endpoints: strength = deep integration with AWS ecosystem and IAM/KMS. Weakness = high egress and cross-account complexity, limited rollout primitives, and opaque autoscaling during correlated bursts. Win theme: emphasize Redwood’s predictable reserved capacity + VPC/private control plane.
- GCP-managed endpoints: strength = near-term developer productivity and BigQuery/Vertex AI integrations. Weakness = mixed performance across GPUs for long-context workloads and limited KV/prefix caching controls. Win theme: highlight Redwood runtime optimizations for long-context KV caching and quantization paths.
- Azure-managed endpoints: strength = enterprise contracts and identity integrations. Weakness = region availability differences and conservative kernel selection leading to higher latency for custom models. Win theme: underscore Redwood’s kernel/compiler tuning and model profiling that reduces per-token cost.

Sales plays and positioning (framed by buyer concerns):
- Cost predictability play (Platform Eng): present a 3-year TCO scenario comparing hyperscaler pay-as-you-go + egress vs Redwood reserved/dedicated with autoscale buffers. Use simple numbers: token cost variance, egress, reserved vs burst. Emphasize cap on tail spend via reserved pools.
- Migration-risk-limiter play (Engineering Leadership): offer migration blueprint: sample infra diagram (VPC peering, private control plane), data-flow trobleshooting checklist, and rollback policy templates. Sell the ability to run side-by-side during migration.
- Compliance-first play (Security/Legal): show architecture for on-prem/private control plane, KMS/HSM integration, audit logs retention options. Provide SOC/ISO checklist and partner references.
- Resilience & fallback play (SRE): discuss multi-tier fallback (model variant fallback, region fallback, capacity-tier fallback) and show sample SLOs with automated fallback policy configurations.

Objection handling (concise counters):
- “Hyperscaler is simpler now” -> Counter: for PoC yes; for production, simplicity hides tail risk. Offer a proof-of-concept that demonstrates production traffic and exposes cost/latency tails in 2 weeks.
- “We need deep cloud integrations” -> Counter: Redwood supports first-class integrations (VPC, KMS, private peering), plus a private deployment option to keep control plane local.
- “Azure/AWS/GCP discounts are better” -> Counter: discounts help but don’t eliminate egress and operational cost volatility; show comparative model: committed reserved pricing + optimizer gains from caching and batching.

Field collateral snippets (one-liners for decks/emails):
- “Reduce inference spend surprises: reserved capacity for predictable tails and automatic cache-aware batching.”
- “Keep the same developer API across hosted, private, and on-prem—avoid rewrite risk during scale.”
- “Rollout with confidence: canaries + eval suites + automatic rollback when quality drops.”

Technical detail bullets to arm SEs (short):
- KV cache lifetime tuning: discuss client-side TTL, shard affinity, and cold-start amplification.
- Quantization fallback: how Redwood maintains accuracy with int8/4 while offering model variants for fallback.
- Network patterns: recommend VPC peering over public egress; include NAT/Gateway considerations and egress cost mitigation tips.
- Observability hooks: token-level cost traces, per-route percentile latency heatmaps, and eval-linked regression alerts.

Demo/POC checklist for closing (two-week sprint):
- Week 0: discover SLA targets, dataset size, token distribution.
- Week 1: run litmus test traffic (synthetic production pattern), collect tail-latency and egress metrics; enable KV caching and measure delta.
- Week 2: configure canary rollout with eval set; simulate model rollback. Deliver TCO comparison and resilience report.

One-page battlecard (talking points):
- Problem statement: Hyperscalers minimize friction for early adoption but amplify cost and availability risks at production scale.
- Redwood advantage: explicit operational levers (reserved capacity, private control plane, rollout policies) that materially reduce risk to product uptime and unit economics.
- Demo ask: show us your production SLA and a week of traffic — we’ll run a focused PoC and a cost/latenct report in 10 business days.

Next steps (tactical):
- Convert this note into a 1-page slide and a 1-page sheet (TCO model template) for AE use.
- Build an SE cheat sheet with the POC checklist and 3 short scripts (cost play, compliance play, resilience play).
- Feed top objection patterns to product for upcoming feature prioritization (especially rollout configurability and per-tenant autoscale profiles).

Open questions we should validate with engineering:
- Provide an exact failure-mode taxonomy timeline for region-level failover (what’s the expected RTO when shifting to a different endpoint/variant?).
- Clarify KMS/HSM onboarding steps for private deployments and estimated lead time.

Notes to self / discussion points for next sync:
- Put customers who hit egress surprises into a case-study bucket (quantify before/after).
- Work with finance to produce a standardized egress offset table by cloud region and provider.

References and signals: attach customer anecdotes, POC numbers, and a short list of hyperscaler docs we commonly cross-reference (kept in linked_artifacts).

End of draft.
